## Course Information

**MATH 435: Mathematical Imaging**

(3 Lecture hours, 0 Laboratory hours, 3 Credits)

## Prerequisites

- (MATH 231 or MATH 232), MATH 315, and one of MATH 242, MATH 243, or MATH 244

## Course Catalog Description

This course introduces the mathematical foundations of imaging science from an inverse problems perspective. It covers image formation, reconstruction, and degradation using tools from linear algebra, Fourier analysis, probability, and optimization. Regularization methods and computational techniques for stable image reconstruction are studied. Applications focus on medical and scientific imaging.

## Textbook

- M. Bertero, P. Boccacci, and C. De Mol, Introduction to Inverse Problems in Imaging, 2nd ed. Boca Raton, FL, USA: CRC Press, 2021.

## Reference Materials

- A. Chambolle and T. Pock, “*An introduction to continuous optimization for imaging*,” *Acta Numerica*, vol. 25, pp. 161–319, 2016.

- S. Mallat, *A Wavelet Tour of Signal Processing*, 3rd ed. Burlington, MA, USA: Academic Press, 2009.

- L. Najman, [<u>Mathematical Imaging</u>](https://lnajman.github.io/math435-mathematical-imaging/book/index.html), online course book for MATH 435.

## Course Structure & Learning Methodology

Lectures are 2 × 75 minutes per week. Lectures are presented using slides and whiteboard. The course is facilitated by computational demonstrations. A team modeling project is conducted throughout the semester to reinforce understanding.

## Course Topics

| **Week \#** | **Topics** |
|:--:|----|
| 01 | Image formation models; convolution; linear systems |
| 02 | Fourier transform; convolution theorem; frequency interpretation of blur |
| 03 | Discrete Fourier transform (DFT); spectral analysis; filtering |
| 04 | Noise models: Gaussian and Poisson; likelihood formulation |
| 05 | Ill-posed inverse problems; instability; SVD (conceptual) |
| 06 | Tikhonov regularization; parameter effects; bias–variance tradeoff |
| 07 | Variational models; convexity (geometric view); Euler–Lagrange derivation |
| 08 | Total Variation regularization; edge preservation; comparison with ℓ2 |
| 09 | Convex optimization basics; gradient descent; proximal ideas |
| 10 | Sparse reconstruction; ℓ1 regularization; compressed sensing intuition |
| 11 | Wavelets and multiscale representations; thresholding |
| 12 | Modern computational imaging: model-based vs data-driven reconstruction |
| 13 | Plug-and-play priors; learned regularization; CNNs as iterative operators |
| 14 | Stability, robustness, and limitations of AI-based reconstruction |
| 15 | Project presentations and oral defenses |

## Laboratory and/or Computing/Digital Resources

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib).

## Instructor Policy on Late Submission of Assignments

**Quizzes** • There will be no make-up quizzes. If the student fails to attend a scheduled quiz <u>without</u> an approved absence from the Student Success Department, then a grade of zero for that quiz will be assigned.

• If the student fails to attend a quiz and the **Student Success Department** **<u>confirms</u>** that the student's absence from that quiz is approved, then the grade that will be assigned to that quiz is

– the grade of the Semester examination if that quiz took place before the Semester examination;

– the grade of the Final Examination if that quiz took place after the Semester examination.

**Semester examination** • There will be no make-up Semester Examination. If the student fails to attend the scheduled Semester examination <u>without</u> an approved absence from the Student Success Department, then a grade of zero will be assigned for the Semester examination.

• If the student fails to attend the Semester examination and the **Student Success Department** **<u>confirms</u>** that the absence from the Semester examination is approved, then the grade for the Final Examination will also be assigned as the grade for the Semester examination.

<u>A maximum of 40% of the course grade can be compensated through the above policy</u>

## Practice and feedback

Short, ungraded exercises on convolution, Fourier filtering and regularization provide practice before graded assessments. Students will receive instructor feedback through discussion or model solutions. The project develops from assignment in week 6 to a brief progress draft in week 8, feedback by week 9, the final report and code in week 14, and individual oral presentations in week 15. The progress draft carries no separate grade.

## Reading guidance and schedule

The [<u>Mathematical Imaging online book</u>](https://lnajman.github.io/math435-mathematical-imaging/book/index.html) is the main weekly reading guide. Read the linked chapter alongside the slides and runnable notebook. This syllabus specifies the prerequisites, assessment weights, deadlines and course policies. The linked online materials support learning.

The plan contains 15 teaching blocks. Semester-specific dates will be mapped to the university academic calendar, including holidays, Innovation Week and the final examination period. Any necessary scheduling adjustments will be communicated through the course learning platform.

## Additional information

### Assessment

Late submission of the group project will not be accepted.

### Project

The project will be assigned in Week 6 of the semester. Students will work in pairs (teams of two) to formulate, analyze, and solve a mathematical imaging reconstruction problem. Each team will develop an appropriate mathematical model, implement computational reconstruction methods, analyze the results, and evaluate model performance and parameter sensitivity.

A brief, ungraded progress draft is due in Week 8. It should identify the forward model, proposed reconstruction method and initial computational results. Feedback will be provided by Week 9 to guide the final report and code.

Students are required to use Python for all computational implementations and analyses.

A written report and the corresponding code must be submitted in Week 14.

In Week 15, each team will participate in an individual oral presentation. Each student will be examined separately on the modeling decisions, implementation, and interpretation of results. Both students are expected to demonstrate full understanding of the entire project.

Failure to participate in the oral presentation will result in a maximum of 50% of the project grade.

Students may use computational tools and AI assistance for the project, but must be able to justify and defend all modeling decisions during the oral presentation.

### Calculator Policy

You will be permitted to only use a basic calculator in the Quizzes, Semester examination and the Final Examination.

### Classroom Policies

Discipline is one of the main components of your academic and professional success.

Please arrive at the class periods in a timely fashion. Students arriving late to class are a distraction to both the instructor and the other students in the classroom.

Please ensure that you sign your name on the Attendance register. If you do not sign the Attendance register, then you will be marked “Absent” in the Banner.

**If you are absent for any lecture, it is your responsibility to cover the missed material.**
